persistence_map — 2D morphology op

• Data kinds: image → image

• Call: fullseye.apply(img, "persistence_map", a=0.5, b=0.5) (the 2-D model is one image plus two scalar knobs a,b∈[0,1])

*The 4th column is a colour (H,W,3) input. This op handles colour without crossing channels (it does not convolve the colour channel as a third spatial axis).*

Usage

Measures the "prominence of peaks" without choosing a threshold (0-dimensional persistence).

Picking a single threshold narrows the range of applicability —— this contradiction is resolved by "trying every threshold and keeping only what does not change". Lower the water level from the top; the difference between the height at which a new peak appears (birth) and the height at which that peak is swallowed by a higher one (death) is taken as that peak's persistence (how much it stands out). It is exactly what topography calls "prominence".

The output is a map holding at each pixel "the persistence of the peak that pixel belongs to". a is the lower limit to keep (peaks below it are set to 0), b the connectivity (below 0.5 a 4-neighbourhood, otherwise an 8-neighbourhood).

h_maxima / MSER compared: xsk2_h_maxima picks one h and returns "the peaks at least that high" —— that is, it picks one threshold. This op folds the answers for every h into a single image, so you can cut at any level you like afterwards. MSER looks for "regions whose area is stable", a similar idea, but it is about region shape whereas this op is about height.

Applicability: (1) The highest peak of the whole image never dies, so max - min is taken as its persistence (by convention). Hence the background holds the global maximum value (1.0) —— the background is processed last, when all components have already merged, so topologically it does belong to the global component. It is a map for reading peak heights, not a map that sets the background to 0. To drop the background, multiply by a threshold op or raise the lower limit with a (measured: with a=0.45 only the peak of height 0.3 vanishes, while 1.0 and 0.6 remain). (2) A flat plateau (a run of equal values) is treated as one peak. (3) The computation is a union-find that scans pixels in descending order, so on large images it is slower than h_maxima.
